title: Managing invigilation and preventing examination malpractice
description: A practical guide for Kenyan senior school principals on structuring invigilation and exam room management to prevent malpractice before it happens.
body:
Examination malpractice carries severe consequences in Kenya — for individual students, whose results can be cancelled, and for schools, whose reputation and even registration can be affected by a serious integrity breach. Most malpractice is preventable through careful invigilation design, not detected after the fact through investigation.

Prevention through room design

Adequate spacing between candidates, assigned seating based on a seating plan rather than free choice, and clear sightlines for invigilators are the foundational physical measures that make malpractice considerably harder to attempt. A seating plan that mixes candidates from different classes or streams, rather than grouping close friends together, further reduces opportunity for collusion.

Invigilator briefing and rotation

Invigilators who are well briefed on what to watch for — unusual movement, unauthorised materials, communication between candidates — perform their role far more effectively than those given only general instructions. Rotating invigilators between rooms across different assessment sessions, rather than always assigning the same person to the same room, reduces the risk of familiarity-based complacency or, in rare cases, collusion between an invigilator and specific candidates.

Practical standard: No invigilator should supervise an examination room containing their own close relative or a student they have a known personal conflict of interest with. This should be checked and adjusted in the invigilation roster before the assessment period, not discovered as a problem afterward.

Clear protocols for suspected incidents

Invigilators who are uncertain what to do when they suspect malpractice often hesitate, allowing an incident to continue or evidence to be lost. A clear, written protocol — exactly what to do, who to notify, how to document an observation — removes this uncertainty and ensures a consistent response regardless of which invigilator is present.

Managing electronic devices and unauthorised materials

Clear, consistently enforced rules on what students may bring into the examination room — with genuine, visible checks at the entry point rather than a nominal rule rarely enforced — prevent the most common and preventable category of malpractice. A rule that is sometimes enforced and sometimes not teaches students that the real risk of being caught is low.

Addressing the underlying pressure that drives malpractice

Malpractice is sometimes a response to genuine desperation under academic pressure, not simple dishonesty. Schools that combine strong integrity enforcement with genuine academic support for struggling students — so that students have a legitimate path to improvement rather than feeling malpractice is their only option — address both the symptom and a root cause simultaneously.

Documentation and fair process

When malpractice is suspected, a documented, fair process — clear evidence recorded at the time, the student given an opportunity to respond, decisions made through proper channels rather than unilaterally — protects both the integrity of the assessment and the rights of the student involved, regardless of the eventual outcome.
